learn.title: Small, complete deliverables
learn.body: A large request hides many decisions and is hard to review. Split it into slices that each produce a useful result, such as one calculation, one screen or one storage change. A slice should have a clear done condition.

learn.title: Agree on interfaces
learn.body: An interface is the agreement where two parts meet. It names the inputs, outputs and expected behavior. For example, a streak function might accept completed dates and return a number. Clear interfaces let slices fit together without guesswork.

learn.title: Look for independence
learn.body: Independent slices can proceed without constantly waiting for each other's unfinished work or editing the same area. They still serve one product goal. Shared sample data and an agreed interface can let one part be checked before another is complete.

learn.title: Slice a streak feature
learn.body: A habit tracker needs a streak number on its summary screen.
steps: Agree that the calculation accepts completed dates and returns a streak count.
Build and test the calculation with today, gaps and duplicate dates.
Build the summary display using the agreed calculation and sample dates.
Connect the real stored dates to the same interface.
Review each result, then check the complete feature together.

learn.title: Slice by boundaries, not arbitrary size
learn.body: Counting lines or files does not make tasks independent. If two slices repeatedly change the same logic or need answers from each other, combine them or clarify their contract. Keep integration as an explicit final task.
Ask for a result you can inspect and test before starting the next dependent slice. Small changes make misunderstandings cheaper to correct.

questions.prompt: What makes a work slice useful?
choices: It has a clear result and done condition
It contains as many features as possible
It always changes exactly one file
questions.explanation: A useful slice produces something reviewable and has a clear finish. File counts are not a reliable boundary, and vague behavior invites rework.

questions.prompt: Smaller slices are easier to \_\_ before more work builds on them.
questions.explanation: A small, defined result can be inspected and tested early. This helps catch a misunderstanding before dependent work spreads it.

questions.prompt: Match each slice to a clear deliverable for a habit tracker.
pairs: A tested count for sample dates
A screen showing the returned count
Real entries supplied through the interface
questions.explanation: Each slice produces an observable result. The interface lets the calculation, display and storage fit together before the final combined check.

questions.prompt: Put this slicing workflow in order.
steps: Integrate the parts and test the whole result
questions.explanation: Define the destination first, agree on boundaries next, then review the parts before integration. The whole feature still needs a final check.

questions.prompt: Which pair is most suitable for independent work after an interface is agreed?
choices: A date calculation and a display that uses its result with sample data
Two people rewriting the same saving logic in different ways
A data format and another task that keeps changing that format
Two tasks with no defined inputs or outputs
questions.explanation: The calculation and display can use the same agreed interface and sample data. Shared rewrites and unstable formats create interference rather than independence.

questions.prompt: What word names the agreement that specifies how two software parts connect?
questions.explanation: An interface, or contract, records the expected inputs, outputs and behavior at a boundary. It reduces assumptions between slices.
